chapter_theme: Two invocations to Vishnu, by likeness and by deed, open twenty verses that each set four 'gems' under one predicate: where things are born, how their worth is tested, what adorns, binds, harms or lays waste, and what each thing ends in. Natural images (gems, beasts, crops, fire) sit in the same row as conduct, so that a virtue is shown to have a source, a test and an end like a thing.

0.reading: The invocation sets four likenesses between the world and Mayavan: the moon is like his bright face, the rayed sun like his discus, the lotus flower opening on its stalk in the old-watered field like his eye, and his colour like the fresh bloom of the kaya flower.
0.nuance: The first three likenesses run from the world to the god (the moon resembles his face), the fourth runs back (his colour resembles the flower), so the sky, the field and the bloom are all read as copies of him. The items here count the god's four features, since the comparison is made for them; மதிமன்னு may also be taken as 'in whom wisdom abides', which would leave the moon unnamed and the face without its likeness.

items.claim: his bright face is what the moon resembles
his discus is what the rayed sun resembles
his eye is what the lotus opening on its stalk resembles
his colour resembles the fresh kaya flower

0b.reading: The second invocation names four deeds of the son: he put the earth inside his belly, crossed the whole earth with his foot in three steps, lifted the hill that sheltered the cows from the cold rain, and destroyed the impregnability of Sho.
0b.nuance: It calls the god only மகன், 'the son', and lets the deeds name him: swallowing the earth, the three strides, the lifted hill (Govardhana by tradition) and the fall of சோ (by tradition Bana's fortress). The verse has no count word; the four deeds are four relative clauses closing on the one noun.

items.claim: he took the earth into his belly
he crossed the whole earth with his foot in three steps
he lifted the hill that kept the cold rain off the cows
he destroyed the impregnability of Sho

1.reading: The verse gives four prohibitions: never despise people as lowly; whatever one would gain, never take anything such that the hand of those one should not take from is above one's own; however it burns within, never rage at those born in small houses; and never hastily say what should not be said.
1.nuance: The four gems here are four negative commands, each verb fronted (எள்ளற்க, கொள்ளற்க, சீறற்க, கூறற்க), so the form turns from naming things to naming restraints. The second and third turn on the giver's or the other's standing: the giver's hand placed above the receiver's, and the small house one is born in. சிற்றில் may mean a poor house as much as a low one; the verse restrains contempt for such people rather than ranking them.

items.claim: despising people because they are lowly is forbidden at all times
taking, at any gain, so that the hand of those one should not receive from is above one's own is forbidden
raging at those born in small houses is forbidden, however it burns within
hastily saying what should not be said is forbidden

2.reading: The asunam beast does not live once the drum is beaten, the strong do not live once their spirit is lessened, the bamboo in the dense forest dies once it puts out grain, and nobility does not live once a word unworthy of it is spoken.
2.nuance: Two of the deaths come from outside (the drum, a word) and one from the thing's own fruit (the bamboo dies of seeding), so the verse does not say whether nobility is killed by another's slander or by its own unworthy speech: சொற்பட allows both. The fourth item makes nobility a living thing that can die while its bearer lives.

items.claim: the asunam does not live once the drum sounds
the strong do not live once their heart is lessened
the bamboo dies once grain forms on it
nobility does not live once a word unfit for it is spoken

3.reading: One knows a gem's worth by washing it, a horse's worth after harnessing and mounting it, gold's worth by burning it free of dross, and the use of one's kin by being ruined.
3.nuance: Each worth is known only by an ordeal applied to it, and the last ordeal falls on the tester, not the tested: one learns what kin are worth by suffering ruin oneself. The verb அறிப repeats four times, so the verse is a list of tests rather than of goods.

items.claim: a gem's worth is known by washing it
a horse's worth is known after it is harnessed and ridden
gold's worth is known by burning it clean of dross
the use one has of kin is known by being ruined

4.reading: Fragrant agil is born in the belly of the kalli, bright orpiment in the belly of the deer, costly pearls in the great sea, and no one knows in what family a good woman is born.
4.nuance: The first three are precious things born of mean or unlikely sources (a thorny spurge, an animal's belly, salt water), so the closing question is not idle: a good woman's worth cannot be read off her family. The verse does not rank families; it denies that family predicts the person.

items.claim: agil is born in the belly of the kalli
bright orpiment is born in the deer's belly
costly pearls are born in the great sea
no one knows the family a good woman is born in

5.reading: The bright gem is born of stone, high delight is born of the beloved's word, the way of virtue is born of gentle compassion, and everything is born of wealth.
5.nuance: The last line widens suddenly: after three particular births it makes wealth the source of all things, which sits beside, and does not cancel, the line that gives virtue its own source in அருள். உயர்மதம் is elation, not pride.

items.claim: the bright gem is born of stone
high delight is born of the beloved's word
the way of virtue is born of gentle compassion
everything is born of wealth

6.reading: Faultless conduct is like fortune, living by the right path is like great virtue, taking someone up and then turning one's face from him is like killing him, and going before those who do not esteem one is like degradation.
6.nuance: Two goods are made equal to greater goods, two wrongs to greater wrongs. புலை in the last item is the word for the degraded or outcaste condition, used here as a measure of shame, not as a rule about persons. The text reads மன்னர் ('kings'), so the last item may be going to kings who do not esteem one; tamilvu has முன்னர், 'before', which gives the general sense.

items.claim: faultless conduct is like fortune itself
living by the right path is like great virtue
taking someone up and then withdrawing one's regard is like killing him
going before those who do not esteem one is like degradation

7.reading: There is no sleep for those who plan to steal, none for those who set their heart on a beloved woman, none for those who plan to make bright wealth, and none either for those who guard that wealth.
7.nuance: The thief and the lover lead to the two kinds of rich man, so earning and guarding wealth are ranked with stealing and longing as kinds of sleeplessness. The last item is set apart with உம் ('the guardians too'): having wealth gives no more rest than wanting it.

items.claim: those who plan to steal get no sleep
those whose heart is set on a beloved get no sleep
those who plan to make bright wealth get no sleep
those who guard that wealth get no sleep either

8.reading: Regret over what is past does not show before the learned, failure does not show before those who have set their love on a thing and pursued it, virtue does not show clearly to those who do what is wrong, and before those who rage everything fails to show and is ruined.
8.nuance: Each item is something that does not appear before a kind of person, but the sense turns: the first two are evils kept away by a virtue, the last two are goods hidden by a vice. உறாமுதல் is rare and may mean 'not attaining' or 'the source of loss'; the reading of the second item rests on that guess.

items.claim: regret for what is past does not appear before the learned
failure does not appear before those who love a thing and pursue it
virtue does not show clearly to those who do wrong
everything vanishes and is ruined before the angry

9.reading: They say paddy and sugarcane are the ornament of the land, the lotus the ornament of a pond, modesty the ornament of a woman's beauty, and one's own ornament is virtue for the world one goes to.
9.nuance: The last item turns the ornament inward and forward: the first three adorn something seen, the fourth adorns the self and is worn into the next world. The third item states a gendered norm: modesty is named the ornament of women's beauty, not of the worthy in general.

items.claim: paddy and sugarcane are the ornament of the land
the lotus is the ornament of a pond
modesty is the ornament of a woman's beauty
virtue for the world one goes to is one's own ornament

norm.note: a gender norm of the period: modesty is assigned to women as the ornament of their beauty

10.reading: They bind a bull elephant to a post to stop its rage, bind the great serpent with a mantra, bind the base with iron after goading them, and the worthy are bound by courtesy.
10.nuance: All four are 'binding' (பிணி), so courtesy is placed among restraints: the worthy are not free of control but are controlled by the gentlest means. The base sit between the beasts and the worthy and need iron.

items.claim: the bull elephant is bound to a post to stop its rage
the great serpent is bound by a mantra
the base are bound with iron after being goaded
the worthy are bound by courtesy

11.reading: One must not be embittered by the harsh things others do, must hold as good the good others did, must always let go of one's own anger, and must destroy the deed that wrecks one's prosperity.
11.nuance: The first two items are a pair about others' acts (their harm not resented, their help remembered), the last two about one's own (one's anger, one's ruinous deed). The fourth item uses அடல், 'killing', for a deed, so the restraint asked is violent toward oneself.

items.claim: the harsh things others did must not embitter one
the good others did must be held as good
one's own anger must always be let go
the deed that wrecks one's prosperity must be destroyed

12.reading: All snakes harm with their teeth, the killing elephant with its tusk, women harm with their face when sulking at those they love, and sages give harm by their penance.
12.nuance: Each harms with its own proper organ or power, and the sage's power is the penance itself: the verse sets the ascetic's curse beside the snake's bite as a natural weapon. Women's harm is the sulk at a lover, a small pain placed between two deadly ones.

items.claim: snakes harm with their teeth
the killing elephant harms with its tusk
women harm with their face when they sulk at those they love
sages give harm through their penance

13.reading: A drum is better than a lute out of tune, a woman firm in self-containment is better than men without worth, going hungry is better than eating with one's dignity undone, and entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to.
13.nuance: Each item prefers a plain or painful thing to a fine thing gone wrong: the crude drum to the spoiled lute, hunger to dishonoured food, fire to separation. The second item sets a woman's நிறை above worthless men, so worth outranks sex here. The last makes parting worse than burning.

items.claim: a drum is better than an untuned lute
a woman firm in self-containment is better than men without worth
hunger is better than eating with dignity undone
entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to

14.reading: Liberality grows in the bed of plenty, the throng of kin rises sweetly in the pit of sweet speech, concealment rises in the graceless pit of harsh speech, and begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty.
14.nuance: Every item is a plant in its bed or pit, so dispositions are crops of conditions: plenty grows giving, poverty grows begging. Two are good crops and two bad, and the begging grows 'quickly'. The division of lines 2 and 3 (where வன்சொல் belongs) is not certain.

items.claim: liberality grows in the bed of plenty
the throng of kin rises sweetly in the pit of sweet speech
concealment rises in the graceless pit of harsh speech
begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty

15.reading: If one wants pain, rise to beg; if one wants to last in this world, plant fame; if one wants what goes along with oneself, do virtue; if one wants to win, give up anger.
15.nuance: The first item is irony in the form of the other three: begging is offered as the sure means to the wish for pain. The pattern 'if you want X, do Y' makes each virtue an instrument, and the last one inverts expectation: one wins by giving up anger, not by using it.

items.claim: the one who wants pain should rise to beg
the one who wants to last in this world should plant fame
the one who wants what goes along with him should do virtue
the one who wants to win should give up anger

16.reading: Sailors split the deep of the sea, the man with a leaping horse can break the deep of an army, the man who holds himself swims the faultless deep of penance, and the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
16.nuance: குட்டம் ('depth') is repeated for sea, army, penance and assembly, so the assembly is made as dangerous as the sea or a battle line, and each is crossed only with its own means. தன்னுடையான் is the self-possessed: the means for penance is mastery of oneself.

items.claim: sailors split the deep of the sea
the man with a leaping horse can break through the deep of an army
the self-possessed swims the faultless deep of penance
the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly

17.reading: Friendships end in falsehood, youth's beauty truly ends in old age, wealth, weighed up, ends in excess, and life ends at its own allotted measure.
17.nuance: Each thing carries its own end (இறுவாய்): friendship is undone by its own falsehood, wealth by its own excess, so the first three ends are made from within. Only life's end is a fixed measure, தகுதி, not a fault.

items.claim: friendships end in falsehood
youth's beauty ends in old age
wealth ends in excess
life ends at its own allotted measure

18.reading: Excellent women are the prosperity of a house, being upright is the prosperity of a man's work, people saying 'this king of the angry red spear is good' is the prosperity of the land, and casting off kin is the prosperity of ruin.
18.nuance: The last item is an ironic turn on the predicate: after three things that build, casting off kin 'builds' ruin. The third makes the land's prosperity a matter of the king's name in people's mouths, not of his wealth. The same last line recurs at verse 85.

items.claim: excellent women are the prosperity of a house
being upright is the prosperity of a man's work
people saying the king is good is the prosperity of the land
casting off one's kin brings ruin as its gain

19.reading: If the husband shakes, the doe-like wife trembles; if the learned man shakes, the meaning shakes; if the land he holds is shaken, the king's sceptre shakes; and if the tune shakes, the song shakes too.
19.nuance: Each pair is a dependence: the wife on the husband, the sense on the learned man, the sceptre on the land, the song on the tune. The third reverses the usual order: the king's rule depends on the land, not the land on the king. அதிர் may be 'tremble' or 'roar'; on the second the first item would say that a husband's anger makes his wife tremble.

items.claim: the doe-like wife trembles when her husband shakes
the meaning shakes when the learned man shakes
the king's sceptre shakes when the land he holds is shaken
the song shakes when its tune shakes

20.reading: Lack of a bright-browed wife is waste to a house, lack of friends is waste to the region one travels to, lack of elders is waste to the assembly one sits in, and a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself.
20.nuance: Three items are absences in a place (house, foreign region, assembly); the fourth puts the absence inside the person, so the unlearned body is itself a ruined house. பாழ் is waste ground, not merely loss.

items.claim: lack of a bright-browed wife lays a house waste
lack of friends lays waste the region one goes to
lack of elders lays waste the assembly one sits in
a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself

links.note: Both invocations of the group open on Vishnu's stride across the earth: Thirikadugam counts it among three deeds of the feet, Nanmanikkadigai among four deeds of the 'son'.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two invocations show the counted form fitted to the god before it is fitted to conduct: each book praises him in its own number, three deeds or four.

links.note: The Kural uses the strider of the earth as the measure of what a king free from sloth gains; the invocation worships the stride itself.
links.teaches: The same three steps serve the Kural as a measure of a diligent king's reach and the invocation as an act of the god, so the myth is shared ground between worship and statecraft.
links.list_adds: It puts the stride among three other cosmic deeds (swallowing the earth, lifting the hill, breaking Sho), so the step is one of the god's acts rather than a yardstick of gain.

links.note: The Naladiyar says true living is never to ask even of the dearest; Nanmanikkadigai forbids only taking so that the hand of those one should not receive from is above one's own.
links.teaches: Against the quatrain's ban on all asking, the verse draws the line at the giver: receiving is shameful when the hand above is one that should not be.
links.list_adds: It sets the rule on receiving beside rules against contempt for the lowly and rage at the humble-born, so the shame of the raised hand is one of four checks on rank-pride.

links.note: Kural 969 compares men who die when honour is lost to the yak that dies when its hair is gone; Nanmanikkadigai has the asunam die at the drum and nobility die at an unworthy word.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet says honour's loss kills its owner, and the verse adds that a single unfit word is enough to kill nobility, so the threat is speech, not only deed.
links.list_adds: It sets nobility's death beside three natural deaths (the asunam, the strong, the seeding bamboo), so the word that kills it is ranked with the drum and the bamboo's own fruit as a fatal cause.

links.note: Kural 796 calls ruin a rod that measures one's people; Nanmanikkadigai says the use of kin is known by being ruined, after the washing of gems, riding of horses and burning of gold.
links.teaches: Together they show ruin as an assay: the couplet names its single benefit, and the verse sets it in the craftsman's sequence of tests, where the tester pays the cost.
links.list_adds: It makes testing kin by ruin the last of four assays with gem, horse and gold, so the kin test is the one that burns the tester, not the thing tested.

links.note: The Naladiyar prizes salt born in barren ground above rice from fertile fields and puts the learned of low origin in the highest place; Nanmanikkadigai says agil, orpiment and pearls come from mean sources and no one knows the family a good woman is born in.
links.teaches: Both books use a precious thing from a poor source to cut worth loose from birth, the Naladiyar for the learned man and Nanmanikkadigai for the good woman.
links.list_adds: Its three natural instances (spurge, deer's belly, sea) build to a question rather than a command, so the reader is left unable to trace goodness to a family.

links.note: Kural 959 says a person's words show the lineage he was born in, as a sprout shows the soil; Nanmanikkadigai asks who can know the family a good woman is born in.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the couplet treats the person as evidence of the family, while the verse denies that inference: goodness, like agil from the spurge, does not reveal its stock.
links.list_adds: Its three images of precious things from unlikely sources make the point by pattern: if agil comes from the kalli, the source cannot be read from the product.

links.note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth as the other is not for those without அருள்; Nanmanikkadigai says the way of virtue is born of அருள் and everything is born of wealth.
links.teaches: The same pair of அருள் and பொருள் appears in both, but the verse turns the couplet's two worlds into two sources: one of virtue, one of everything else.
links.list_adds: It sets the pair after the gem from stone and delight from the beloved's word, and closes on wealth as the source of all, which makes the couplet's balance end in wealth's favour.

links.note: Naladiyar 280 says earning, guarding, losing and ruin of wealth are all suffering; Nanmanikkadigai says those who plan to make wealth and those who guard it get no sleep.
links.teaches: The quatrain says wealth is suffering at every stage; the verse names the suffering as sleeplessness and gives it to the thief and the lover as well.
links.list_adds: It ranks the earner and guardian of wealth with the thief and the lovesick as sleepless men, so lawful wealth shares its unrest with theft and longing.

links.note: Thirikadugam 73 names the man who says he will make bright wealth by begging as one who lives daring the hard; Nanmanikkadigai says the one who plans to make bright wealth gets no sleep.
links.teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the plan to make bright wealth and both make it a hardship: Thirikadugam a daring, Nanmanikkadigai a sleepless night.

links.note: Kural 304 says anger kills smile and joy and is the worst enemy; Nanmanikkadigai says before the angry everything fails to show and is ruined.
links.teaches: The couplet names what anger kills in the angry man; the verse widens it to everything before him, so anger blinds as well as destroys.
links.list_adds: It sets anger's ruin after three things that do not show before the learned, the resolved and the wrongdoer, so anger closes a list of what each kind of person cannot see.

links.note: Kural 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of a woman's beauty.
links.teaches: The Kural gives shame to the worthy of either sex as their ornament, while the verse assigns it to women's beauty, so the pair shows the virtue narrowed into a gendered adornment.
links.list_adds: It puts women's modesty in a row of ornaments with paddy for land and lotus for pond, which makes the virtue something that decorates a seen beauty, where the Kural makes it a guard of conduct.

links.note: Thirikadugam 52 calls modesty the ornament of a woman in love and learning the ornament for the next life; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of women's beauty and virtue the ornament for the world one goes to.
links.teaches: Both short works pair a woman's modesty with an ornament for the next life, so the gendered ornament and the otherworldly one are a shared pairing of the group, not one poet's choice.

links.note: Verse 9 calls virtue one's own ornament for the world one goes to; verse 15 says that if one wants what goes along with oneself, one should do virtue.
links.teaches: Within the book virtue is twice the one thing that crosses death, once as an ornament worn and once as a companion that goes along.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Nanmanikkadigai binds the base with iron and the worthy by courtesy.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks of what the two yield; the verse of how they are held, so the pair moves from extracting good to restraining harm with the same contrast.
links.list_adds: It puts the base and the worthy in a row with the raging elephant and the great serpent, so each kind of creature has its own binding and courtesy becomes a bond.

links.note: Kural 108 says it is not good to forget a good done and good to forget at once what is not good; Nanmanikkadigai asks one not to be embittered by harsh acts and to hold the good done as good.
links.teaches: Both pair forgetting injury with remembering help; the verse goes on to one's own anger and ruinous deeds, so the inward work follows the outward.
links.list_adds: It follows the couplet's pair with two rules about oneself (letting anger go, destroying the self-ruining deed), so forgiving others is set beside disciplining oneself.

links.note: Kural 29 says the anger of those who have climbed the hill of virtue is hard to withstand even for a moment; Nanmanikkadigai says sages give harm through their penance.
links.teaches: The couplet warns of the ascetic's anger; the verse names its weapon, penance itself, and sets it with the snake's tooth and the elephant's tusk.
links.list_adds: It ranks the sage's penance with the snake's tooth, the elephant's tusk and the sulking woman's face as four instruments of harm, so holy power is classed as a natural weapon.

links.note: Kural 968 asks whether feeding the body is a medicine once dignity is lost; Nanmanikkadigai says hunger is better than eating with dignity undone.
links.teaches: The couplet questions the worth of a life fed without honour; the verse states the choice as a meal: go hungry rather than eat so.
links.list_adds: It places the choice among three other preferences of the plain over the spoiled (drum over untuned lute, a firm woman over worthless men, fire over parting), so hunger is one of four lesser goods.

links.note: Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, but love burns when one moves away; Nanmanikkadigai says entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to.
links.teaches: Both weigh separation against fire and find separation the worse, the couplet in a lover's voice and the verse as a general rule of attachment.
links.list_adds: It carries the lover's comparison into a list of plain preferences, so parting from one's own becomes a general loss, not only love's.

links.note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is ringed by kin; Nanmanikkadigai says the throng of kin rises in the pit of sweet speech and liberality grows in the bed of plenty.
links.teaches: The couplet gives two causes of a crowd of kin; the verse splits them, puts each in its own soil, and pairs them with the bad crops of harsh speech and poverty.
links.list_adds: It makes each disposition a crop of its condition, two good and two bad, so kin-gathering is shown with its opposite, concealment from harsh speech.

links.note: Naladiyar 306 says poverty can be ended by asking oneself rather than begging from strangers; Nanmanikkadigai says begging springs up quickly in the pit of poverty.
links.teaches: The verse describes begging as poverty's quick crop; the quatrain answers that the crop need not grow if one begs of oneself, so the pair sets the natural course against the discipline that stops it.
links.list_adds: It sets begging as the last of four growths from their soils, so it appears as a natural consequence where the Naladiyar treats it as a choice.

links.note: Kural 36 says to do virtue now, since it is the companion that does not perish when one does; Nanmanikkadigai says that one who wants what goes along with oneself should do virtue.
links.teaches: Both make virtue the one companion past death, and the verse puts it as a means to a wish, beside fame for lasting here and giving up anger for winning.
links.list_adds: Its 'if you want X, do Y' frame sets virtue as the means for one wish among four, with begging as the ironic means to pain, so the virtues become instruments chosen by their ends.

links.note: Verse 11 says one must always let go of one's anger; verse 15 says one who wants to win should give up anger.
links.teaches: The two verses together give the rule and its reason: anger is let go not only as a duty but because giving it up is how one wins.

links.note: Verse 14 says begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty; verse 15 says one who wants pain should rise to beg.
links.teaches: Read together, the book gives begging both a cause and a fruit: it grows from poverty and it yields pain.

links.note: Kural 725 says to learn by the proper path so as to answer without fear in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the purpose of learning as fearless reply; the verse calls the assembly a deep like the sea and a battle line, which shows why that fear is real.
links.list_adds: It ranks the learned man's crossing of the assembly with the sailor's sea, the horseman's army and the ascetic's penance, so speaking before an assembly is made as perilous as war or the sea.

links.note: Thirikadugam 7 names the hard learning of one who fears assemblies as a mute's dream; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
links.teaches: The same claim is put from two sides: learning that fails in the assembly is useless, and learning is what carries a man across it.

links.note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as not lasting, so the best renounce them; Nanmanikkadigai gives friendship, youth, wealth and life each its own end.
links.teaches: The quatrain says these things do not last; the verse says what each ends in, and three of the ends (falsehood, old age, excess) come from the thing itself.
links.list_adds: It assigns each thing its own end, so wealth ends in excess and friendship in falsehood rather than all ending alike, and it adds friendship, which the quatrain does not name.

links.note: Kural 523 says one who does not mingle with kin lives like a tank filling with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai says casting off kin is the gain of ruin.
links.teaches: The couplet shows the loss in an image of wealth spilling away; the verse names it ironically as ruin's prosperity, closing a list of what builds.
links.list_adds: It sets casting off kin after three true sources of prosperity (a good wife, uprightness, a king's good name), so the last item undoes the predicate by calling ruin a gain.

links.note: Kural 386 says the land of an accessible king who is not harsh of speech is spoken of above others; Nanmanikkadigai says the land's prosperity is people saying 'this king is good'.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the king's conduct that earns praise; the verse makes that praise itself the land's wealth.
links.list_adds: It sets the king's good name among the prosperity of house and work, so the realm's gain is one of a household series, measured by speech.

links.note: Verse 18 says excellent women are the prosperity of a house; verse 20 says the lack of a bright-browed wife lays a house waste.
links.teaches: The book states the same claim from both sides, prosperity with a good wife and waste without one, so the house is defined by the wife's presence.

links.note: Verse 16 says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly; verse 19 says that if the learned man shakes, the meaning shakes.
links.teaches: The book qualifies its praise of the learned: he carries the meaning across the assembly only while he holds firm, and his faltering loses it.

links.note: Kural 406 likens the unlearned to barren saline ground; Nanmanikkadigai says a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself.
links.teaches: Both use waste land for the unlearned, but the couplet says they yield nothing to others while the verse says the body is waste to its owner.
links.list_adds: It sets the unlearned body after a house without a wife, a region without friends and an assembly without elders, so the ignorant self is one of four places laid waste by an absence.

links.note: Thirikadugam 10 names an assembly with no elders to settle quarrels among three things that yield no good; Nanmanikkadigai calls lack of elders waste to the assembly.
links.teaches: Both short works make elders the thing an assembly cannot do without, and Thirikadugam gives the reason the verse omits: elders settle disputes.

source_issues: 0 and 0b: the book opens with two invocations, keyed 0 and 0b.

10 line 3 and 20 line 2: stray spaces split words (சான் றோரை, நட்டோ ரை).
